newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Strong A$ seen having mild effect on equities.
newsitem.headline: Strong A$ seen having mild effect on equities.

text.p: The strong rise in the Australian dollar late last week will further dampen an already cautious earnings outlook for Australian companies if the currency stays at current levels, Australian equity analysts and strategists said.

But the rise in the "Aussie" also means that Australian assets are in demand so volumes should rise and balance any negative effect on corporate profits from a stronger local dollar against the U.S. dollar, they said.
The Australian dollar has risen three cents over the past fortnight against the U.S. dollar and was quoted at US$8095/00 late on Friday afternoon.
"It does put pressure on profit margins on some of the large companies," said John Banos, equity strategist at brokerage firm McIntosh Securities.

"On the industrial side this does put a big squeeze on all the companies with offshore earnings, it is a negative influence, it is one of the factors that mean the market is a bit weaker today," Banos told Reuters.
The sharemarket ended nine points down at 2,383.4 oon Friday.
Analysts said firms with significant overseas operations such as News Corp Ltd and the major Australian banks are likely to the most affected by a stronger local currency.

The effect on miners will be at best neutral as higher commodity prices, which are helping the currency rise, will increase profits for the sector. But the gains would be somewhat muted when they are converted into local dollars, analysts said. recently, while nickel has just come off its two-year lows, and lead and zinc have remained relatively steady.

"It's a mild negative, particularly on the resources side, and the market has generally factored in a 79 cent currency so 81 plus is a mild negative," said Craig Drummond, head of equity research at Melbourne-based brokers J.B. Were & Son.
"A lot of this move has been over the past week, so in the short term I don't think we are going have any analysts downgrading their estimates," Drummond told Reuters.
He said if the Australian dollar stayed at current levels for the next two months then analysts would start to lower their earnings estimates for the 1996/97 year.

Australian companies over the past couple of months have been cautious about their earnings outlook for 1996/97 due to a slowing Australian economy and the higher Australian dollar, even before the recent hike.
Many chief executives blamed the stronger dollar for their company's disappointing results in 1995/96, when it averaged about US$0.76 up from the average of $0.74 cents in 1994/95.
However, analysts said the stronger dollar often equates to a stronger sharemarket, if history is anything to go by.
"In general a strong currency means a strong equity market even though the underlying fundamentals are probably suffering a little bit," J.B. Were's Drummond said.
David Rickards, an equities strategist at Macquarie Equities said: "I haven't heard of any country going broke from a strong currency."

"Companies are helped by a stronger currency, because the stronger currency is reflecting that the country is worth more and someone from offshore is willing to pay more for an Australian asset," Rickards told Reuters.
However, the rise in the local dollar has caught many firms by surprise as many currency traders have said that firms have not had adequate hedging in place.
Traders said the dollar's rise is also due to the higher Australian interest rates compared with other industrialised nations.
"The danger is that you get the Australian dollar going up for reasons unrelated to the commodity price," said Marcus Tuck, an economist at brokers HSBC James Capel.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
